claim: goa-1(n1134) retains few eggs in the uterus and is associated with a significantly lower number of ALMR exopher events as compared to the age-matched wild-type control.
source: We confirmed that goa-1(n1134) retains few eggs in the uterus and is associated with a significantly lower number of ALMR exopher events as compared to the age-matched wild-type control (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Manipulation of uterine egg occupancy is strongly correlated with the extent of ALMR neuronal exophergenesis—high egg retention promotes high exophergenesis and low egg retention is associated with low exophergenesis.
source: In sum, manipulation of uterine egg occupancy is strongly correlated with the extent of ALMR neuronal exophergenesis—high egg retention promotes high exophergenesis and low egg retention is associated with low exophergenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The ALML and ALMR anterior touch neurons share developmental, morphological, and functional similarities.
source: The ALML and ALMR anterior touch neurons share developmental, morphological, and functional similarities (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981), yet paradoxically, ALMR consistently produces exophers at higher levels than ALML (Melentijevic et al., 2017; also Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981).

claim: ALMR consistently produces exophers at higher levels than ALML.
source: The ALML and ALMR anterior touch neurons share developmental, morphological, and functional similarities (Chalfie and Sulston, 1981), yet paradoxically, ALMR consistently produces exophers at higher levels than ALML (Melentijevic et al., 2017; also Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Melentijevic et al., 2017) and experimental data in Figure 4G.

claim: The ALMR soma is situated in the vicinity of the gonad and its resident eggs, whereas the ALML soma, on the opposite side of the animal, is positioned closer to the intestine.
source: The ALM neurons are embedded within the C. elegans hypodermis, but the ALMR soma is situated in the vicinity of the gonad and its resident eggs, whereas the ALML soma, on the opposite side of the animal, is positioned closer to the intestine (Figure 4A and B; Goodman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical diagrams in Figures 4A and 4B and citation (Goodman, 2006).

claim: 36/37 (95%) of the Exopher+ ALMR neuronal somas that had produced exophers were positioned within the visualized egg zone.
source: We found that 37/128 ALMRs examined had produced an exopher (Exopher+), and that 36/37 (95%) of the Exopher+ ALMR neuronal somas that had produced exophers were positioned within the visualized egg zone (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For the Exopher- ALMRs that had not produced exophers, 63/91 (70%) had neuronal somas located in the egg zone.
source: For the Exopher- ALMRs that had not produced exophers, 63/91 (70%) had neuronal somas located in the egg zone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Although ALMR soma positioning in the egg zone does not guarantee exophergenesis in the mCherryAg2 strain, the neurons that did make exophers were nearly always in the egg zone (p<0.01 in Chi-Square test).
source: Thus, although ALMR soma positioning in the egg zone does not guarantee exophergenesis in the mCherryAg2 strain, the neurons that did make exophers were nearly always in the egg zone (p<0.01 in Chi-Square test, Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Transgenic introduction of a mec-3 promoter fragment bearing an internal deletion (fusion of the –1 to –563 sequences to the –1898 to –2372 mec-3 promoter fragment, plasmid pJC4) can induce anterior ALM migration during development, sometimes resulting in final ALM positions anterior to AVM.
source: In particular, transgenic introduction of a mec-3 promoter fragment bearing an internal deletion (fusion of the –1 to –563 sequences to the –1898 to –2372 mec-3 promoter fragment, plasmid pJC4) can induce anterior ALM migration during development, sometimes resulting in final ALM positions anterior to AVM (Toms et al., 2001; Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Toms et al., 2001).

claim: Rol hermaphrodites have a strikingly high baseline of ALMR exophergenesis (approximately 40% exophers in rollers vs. approximately 20% in the wild-type).
source: Rol hermaphrodites have a strikingly high baseline of ALMR exophergenesis (~40% exophers in rollers vs. ~20% in the wild-type).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the pJC4 + rol-6(su1006) strain.

claim: When ALMs are situated anterior to AVM, ALMR exophergenesis drops to approximately 5% (4/73) vs 71% for the posterior position (55/78).
source: Strikingly, we found that when ALMs are situated anterior to AVM, ALMR exophergenesis drops to ~5% (4/73) vs 71% for the posterior position (55/78) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the sem-2(rf) background, every touch neuron that is positioned in the general region of the expanded uterus (ALML, AVM, PVM) increases exopher production, but the posterior PLM neurons, which cannot be approached by the gonad, do not produce exophers.
source: Indeed, we find that in the sem-2(rf) background, every touch neuron that is positioned in the general region of the expanded uterus (ALML, AVM, PVM) increases exopher production, but the posterior PLM neurons, which cannot be approached by the gonad, do not produce exophers (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Touch neurons can be stimulated to produce exophers if the egg domain is artificially brought closer to them.
source: Thus, touch neurons can be stimulated to produce exophers if the egg domain is artificially brought closer to them.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 4G showing increased exophers in multiple touch neurons when the uterus expands.

claim: ALMR normally makes most exophers because of its closest natural positioning near the egg-filled uterus.
source: Data are consistent with a model in which ALMR normally makes most exophers because of its closest natural positioning near the egg-filled uterus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 4 showing correlation between proximity to eggs and exopher production.

claim: Eggs can readily be observed to distort tissue structure in young adult C. elegans.
source: Eggs can readily be observed to distort tissue structure in young adult C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The uterus can approach and pressure surrounding tissue, including touch neurons.
source: Thus, the uterus can approach and pressure surrounding tissue, including touch neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations in Figure 5A showing tissue distortion by eggs.

claim: Egg retention mutants that exhibit high exophergenesis, egl-3(Δ), egl-9(Δ), and sem-2(rf), had significantly longer egg zones (i.e. uterus length) as compared to wild-type.
source: We found that egg retention mutants that exhibit high exophergenesis, egl-3(Δ) (Figure 5B), egl-9(Δ) (Figure 5C), and sem-2(rf) (Figure 5D), had significantly longer egg zones (i.e. uterus length) as compared to wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: cbd-1 RNAi, sperm-less induction with SPE-44 AID, and hyperactive egg-laying mutant goa-1(Δ), which are strong exophergenesis suppressors, are all associated with short uterine egg zones.
source: In contrast, cbd-1 RNAi (Figure 5E), sperm-less induction with SPE-44 AID (Figure 5F), and hyperactive egg-laying mutant goa-1(Δ) (Figure 5G), which we find to be strong exophergenesis suppressors, are all associated with short uterine egg zones.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E-G.

claim: Knocking down either the 4 cell stage gene mex-3 or the gastrulation gene gad-1, which are associated with neither egg retention nor exopher elevation, does not have an extended egg zone/uterine length.
source: Knocking down either the 4 cell stage gene mex-3 or the gastrulation gene gad-1, which are associated with neither egg retention nor exopher elevation, does not have an extended egg zone/uterine length (Figure 5H), so not all developmental compromises are associated with uterine extension.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Not all developmental compromises are associated with uterine extension.
source: Knocking down either the 4 cell stage gene mex-3 or the gastrulation gene gad-1, which are associated with neither egg retention nor exopher elevation, does not have an extended egg zone/uterine length (Figure 5H), so not all developmental compromises are associated with uterine extension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 5H.

claim: Under conditions of cbd-1 RNAi, eggshell development and embryonic development are blocked.
source: Under conditions of cbd-1 RNAi, eggshell development and embryonic development are blocked; eggs that form are fragile and can be malformed consequent to passing through the spermatheca into the uterus; embryonic development does not proceed and egg remnants tend to be sticky (Johnston et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Johnston et al., 2010).

claim: Treating WT reproductive animals (that have functional egg-laying capacity) with cbd-1 RNAi to kill embryos exerts a potent block on ALMR exophergenesis.
source: As shown in Figure 2B (and again in Figure 6A), treating WT reproductive animals (that have functional egg-laying capacity) with cbd-1 RNAi to kill embryos exerts a potent block on ALMR exophergenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 6A.

claim: cbd-1 RNAi/dead embryo retention in the sem-2(rf) background is still associated with significantly elevated levels of ALMR exophergenesis (approximately 45%), while in egg-laying proficient wild-type, barely any ALMR exophergenesis is observed under cbd-1 RNAi conditions (<1%).
source: Strikingly, we found that cbd-1 RNAi/dead embryo retention in the sem-2(rf) background is still associated with significantly elevated levels of ALMR exophergenesis (~45%), while in egg-laying proficient wild-type, barely any ALMR exophergenesis is observed under cbd-1 RNAi conditions (<1%) (69/150 for sem-2 egg-laying blocked cbd-1 RNAi vs. 1/150 for egg-laying proficient cbd-1 RNAi, Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Under conditions of defective eggshell/dead embryo retention associated with cbd-1 RNAi; sem-2(rf), the uterine egg zone is expanded.
source: Importantly, under conditions of defective eggshell/dead embryo retention associated with cbd-1 RNAi; sem-2(rf), the uterine egg zone is expanded (Figure 6B), extending the correlation of exopher production with uterine length.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Intact eggshells and earliest embryonic divisions are not required for the boost in exopher production observed when uterine contents are forced to accumulate.
source: We conclude that intact eggshells and earliest embryonic divisions are not required for the boost in exopher production observed when uterine contents are forced to accumulate—uterine retention of dead eggs and egg remnants is sufficient for exopher elevation if the egg laying apparatus is defective.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 6A showing high exophers with cbd-1 RNAi in sem-2(rf) background.

claim: Uterine retention of dead eggs and egg remnants is sufficient for exopher elevation if the egg laying apparatus is defective.
source: We conclude that intact eggshells and earliest embryonic divisions are not required for the boost in exopher production observed when uterine contents are forced to accumulate—uterine retention of dead eggs and egg remnants is sufficient for exopher elevation if the egg laying apparatus is defective.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 6A.

claim: Expansion of the uterine compartment, rather than eggshell/embryo integrity, tracks with exopher elevation.
source: Expansion of the uterine compartment, rather than eggshell/embryo integrity, tracks with exopher elevation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Unfertilized oocytes cannot initiate embryonic development or egg-shell biosynthesis.
source: Unfertilized oocytes cannot initiate embryonic development or egg-shell biosynthesis; nor can oocytes elevate ALMR exophergenesis in hermaphrodites that are proficient at egg-laying (Figure 1G&H).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of C. elegans reproductive biology.

claim: Oocytes cannot elevate ALMR exophergenesis in hermaphrodites that are proficient at egg-laying.
source: Unfertilized oocytes cannot initiate embryonic development or egg-shell biosynthesis; nor can oocytes elevate ALMR exophergenesis in hermaphrodites that are proficient at egg-laying (Figure 1G&H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: In the absence of sperm, oocytes do not mature but are 'ovulated' at a reduced rate compared to in the presence of sperm.
source: Note that in the absence of sperm, oocytes do not mature but are 'ovulated' at a reduced rate compared to in the presence of sperm; oogenesis continues such that ~25 oocytes are typically found stacked in the gonad (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; McGovern et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (McGovern et al., 2007) and observations in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oogenesis continues in the absence of sperm such that approximately 25 oocytes are typically found stacked in the gonad.
source: Note that in the absence of sperm, oocytes do not mature but are 'ovulated' at a reduced rate compared to in the presence of sperm; oogenesis continues such that ~25 oocytes are typically found stacked in the gonad (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; McGovern et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (McGovern et al., 2007) and observations in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Build-up of retained oocytes in egg-laying blocked animals was both sufficient to elevate exophers and expand the uterus.
source: For both genetic retention strategies, we found that build-up of retained oocytes in egg-laying blocked animals was both sufficient to elevate exophers (Figure 6C&E) and expand the uterus (Figure 6D&F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C-F.

claim: The oocyte retention was similarly efficacious in elevating exopher production to egg retention, increasing ALMR exophergenesis to approximately 80% in the sem-2(rf) mutant.
source: Moreover, the oocyte retention was similarly efficacious in elevating exopher production to egg retention, increasing ALMR exophergenesis to approximately 80% in the sem-2(rf) mutant (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Fertilization, egg shells, and egg remnants are not essential for the early adult exopher peak.
source: We conclude that fertilization, egg shells, and egg remnants are not essential for the early adult exopher peak.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6C and 6E showing high exophers with oocyte retention.

claim: Expansion of the uterus with unfertilized oocytes can suffice to elevate neuronal exopher formation.
source: Expansion of the uterus with unfertilized oocytes can suffice to elevate neuronal exopher formation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6C-F.

claim: lin-39 RNAi + oocyte retention promotes exopher formation, but eliminating oocytes (fem-3(gf)) eliminates exopher elevation even when egg-laying is blocked by lin-39 RNAi.
source: lin-39 RNAi + oocyte retention promotes exopher formation, but eliminating oocytes (fem-3(gf)) eliminates exopher elevation even when egg-laying is blocked by lin-39 RNAi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Although oocyte accumulation with uterine expansion suffices to elevate exophers, removing the oocytes and uterus occupancy eliminates the exopher boost.
source: That is to say, although oocyte accumulation with uterine expansion suffices to elevate exophers, removing the oocytes and uterus occupancy eliminates the exopher boost.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 6G.

claim: Disruption of egg laying on its own is not the driving factor in high exophergenesis; rather, uterine filling is required.
source: Thus, disruption of egg laying on its own is not the driving factor in high exophergenesis; rather, uterine filling is required.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6G and 6H showing that blocking egg-laying without uterine filling does not induce exophers.

claim: ALMR exophergenesis is strongly correlated with the level of uterus stretching caused by the accumulation of uterine contents.
source: We revisited the relationship of uterine length and exopher level by adding data from the studies with oocyte retention to reinforce the conclusion that ALMR exophergenesis is strongly correlated with the level of uterus stretching caused by the accumulation of uterine contents (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I demonstrating correlation between uterine length and exopher levels.

claim: When 2 or more minutes of injection pressure was held continuously, approximately 20% of the ALMs scored exhibited an exopher event shortly after injection.
source: We found that when we held injection pressure continuously for 2 or more minutes, ~20% of the ALMs scored exhibited an exopher event shortly after injection (Figure 7C&D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Injection experiments using animals with functional vulvae (in which injected material is rapidly extruded through the vulval opening) failed to induce ALMR exophers.
source: Injection experiments using animals with functional vulvae (in which injected material is rapidly extruded through the vulval opening) failed to induce ALMR exophers (Figure 7E), supporting that ALMR exophergenesis caused by 2 min injection of dye-containing M9 is due to the physical distortion of gonad rather than the chemical impact of the dye-containing M9.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: ALMR exophergenesis caused by 2 min injection of dye-containing M9 is due to the physical distortion of gonad rather than the chemical impact of the dye-containing M9.
source: Injection experiments using animals with functional vulvae (in which injected material is rapidly extruded through the vulval opening) failed to induce ALMR exophers (Figure 7E), supporting that ALMR exophergenesis caused by 2 min injection of dye-containing M9 is due to the physical distortion of gonad rather than the chemical impact of the dye-containing M9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 7E.

claim: Exopher induction by uterine accumulation of eggs, malformed eggs, dead embryos, oocytes, or fluid-induced expansion supports a model in which early adult ALMR exophergenesis is elevated by physical distortion of the uterus that occurs with reproduction.
source: In sum, exopher induction by uterine accumulation of eggs, malformed eggs, dead embryos, oocytes, or fluid-induced expansion supports a model in which early adult ALMR exophergenesis is elevated by physical distortion of the uterus that occurs with reproduction (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The early exophergenesis peak is dependent on uterine occupation, which normally is conferred by fertilized egg accumulation prior to the deposition of eggs.
source: Here, we report that the early exophergenesis peak is dependent on uterine occupation, which normally is conferred by fertilized egg accumulation prior to the deposition of eggs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cumulative experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Uterine expansion that is associated with the filling of a blocked uterus with unfertilized oocytes or by fluid alone can also induce high neuronal exopher production.
source: Uterine expansion that is associated with the filling of a blocked uterus with unfertilized oocytes or by fluid alone can also induce high neuronal exopher production, supporting a model in which the physical distention associated with uterine occupancy, rather than chemical signals derived from fertilized eggs per se, is a required component of the signaling relay between reproduction and young adult neuronal debris elimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The physical distention associated with uterine occupancy, rather than chemical signals derived from fertilized eggs per se, is a required component of the signaling relay between reproduction and young adult neuronal debris elimination.
source: Uterine expansion that is associated with the filling of a blocked uterus with unfertilized oocytes or by fluid alone can also induce high neuronal exopher production, supporting a model in which the physical distention associated with uterine occupancy, rather than chemical signals derived from fertilized eggs per se, is a required component of the signaling relay between reproduction and young adult neuronal debris elimination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Trans-tissue cross-talk to the maternal nervous system appears accomplished via mechanical force transduction.
source: Trans-tissue cross-talk to the maternal nervous system thus appears accomplished via mechanical force transduction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative experimental data showing mechanical force effects on exopher production.

claim: C. elegans reproduction features physical expansion and contraction of multiple tissue/cell types--the gonad houses the expanding germline, and the spermatheca expands and retracts vigorously as each mature oocyte enters and exits.
source: C. elegans reproduction features physical expansion and contraction of multiple tissue/cell types--the gonad houses the expanding germline, and the spermatheca expands and retracts vigorously as each mature oocyte enters and exits.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of C. elegans reproductive biology.

claim: The uterus stretches to house eggs and can contract locally as eggs transit or are expelled via the action of the vulval and uterine muscles.
source: The uterus also stretches to house eggs and can contract locally as eggs transit or are expelled via the action of the vulval and uterine muscles.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of C. elegans reproductive biology.

claim: The filled reproductive apparatus can exert both constitutive and sporadic pressure on surrounding tissues as it enacts its essential functions.
source: The filled reproductive apparatus can thus clearly exert both constitutive and sporadic pressure on surrounding tissues as it enacts its essential functions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations of tissue distortion by eggs and knowledge of reproductive mechanics.

claim: Elegant work on the egg-laying circuit has provided evidence for mechanical signaling within the egg-laying circuit that regulates initiation, promotion, and termination of egg-laying.
source: Elegant work on the egg-laying circuit (comprising the somatic gonad, the HSN and VC neurons, and the vulval, and uterine muscle) has provided evidence for mechanical signaling within the egg-laying circuit that regulates initiation, promotion, and termination of egg-laying (Medrano and Collins, 2023; Ravi et al., 2018; Kopchock et al., 2021; Ravi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Medrano and Collins, 2023; Ravi et al., 2018; Kopchock et al., 2021; Ravi et al., 2021).

claim: Exopher-promoting force seems unlikely to derive from the vulva or vulval muscle contractions, since when these cells are genetically disrupted in lin-39 RNAi or in sem-2 mutants, high levels of exophers still are generated.
source: Working backward, exopher-promoting force seems unlikely to derive from the vulva or vulval muscle contractions, since when these cells are genetically disrupted in lin-39 RNAi or in sem-2 mutants, high levels of exophers still are generated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 3 and 6 showing high exophers in vulva-defective mutants.

claim: Spermatheca contractions are reported to be normal in hyperactive egg-laying goa-1.
source: Changes in spermatheca volume, which expands and contracts dramatically as mature oocytes enter via valve opening/closure (Tan and Zaidel-Bar, 2015), might be sensed, but spermatheca contractions are reported to be normal in hyperactive egg-laying goa-1 (Govindan et al., 2006), which is an exopher-suppressing background.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Govindan et al., 2006).

claim: Under no-sperm conditions, oocyte transit rates are lower than for fertilized eggs.
source: Under no-sperm conditions, oocyte transit rates are lower than for fertilized eggs, and sperm-derived signals influence spermathecal valve opening (McGovern et al., 2007; McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001), but if the egg-laying apparatus is genetically compromised and oocytes accumulate in the absence of sperm, exopher levels are high, suggesting deficits in spermatheca operations or sperm signals per se do not drive exophergenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (McGovern et al., 2007; McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001).

claim: Sperm-derived signals influence spermathecal valve opening.
source: Under no-sperm conditions, oocyte transit rates are lower than for fertilized eggs, and sperm-derived signals influence spermathecal valve opening (McGovern et al., 2007; McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001), but if the egg-laying apparatus is genetically compromised and oocytes accumulate in the absence of sperm, exopher levels are high, suggesting deficits in spermatheca operations or sperm signals per se do not drive exophergenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (McGovern et al., 2007; McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001).

claim: If the egg-laying apparatus is genetically compromised and oocytes accumulate in the absence of sperm, exopher levels are high, suggesting deficits in spermatheca operations or sperm signals per se do not drive exophergenesis.
source: Under no-sperm conditions, oocyte transit rates are lower than for fertilized eggs, and sperm-derived signals influence spermathecal valve opening (McGovern et al., 2007; McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001), but if the egg-laying apparatus is genetically compromised and oocytes accumulate in the absence of sperm, exopher levels are high, suggesting deficits in spermatheca operations or sperm signals per se do not drive exophergenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figures 6C and 6E.

claim: The simplest model for the reproductive cues that influence maternal neuronal exophergenesis is that a filled uterus (under normal conditions the consequence of hard-shelled eggs that occupy it) is sensed and required for the early adult peak in exopher production.
source: Thus, the simplest model we envision for the reproductive cues that influence maternal neuronal exophergenesis is that a filled uterus (under normal conditions the consequence of hard-shelled eggs that occupy it) is sensed and required for the early adult peak in exopher production.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cumulative experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mechanotransduction is the sensing of a mechanical signal, such as pressure or stretch, and conversion into a cellular response.
source: Mechanotransduction is the sensing of a mechanical signal, such as pressure or stretch, and conversion into a cellular response.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field of mechanobiology.

claim: Members of several ion channel families have been implicated in sensing of touch, hearing, shear stress, and pressure, including Piezo, TRP, and DEG/ENaC families.
source: Members of several ion channel families have been implicated in sensing of touch, hearing, shear stress, and pressure, including Piezo, TRP, and DEG/ENaC families (Delmas and Coste, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Delmas and Coste, 2013).

claim: Classic mechanosensory channels have extremely rapid gating and might not be the best-suited candidates for acting in the sustained and locally dynamic forces anticipated for the reproductive uterine environment.
source: At the same time, classic mechanosensory channels have extremely rapid gating and might not be the best-suited candidates for acting in the sustained and locally dynamic forces anticipated for the reproductive uterine environment.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on knowledge of mechanosensory channel properties.

claim: Adhesion G-Protein Coupled Receptors have extracellular adhesion motifs and seven transmembrane domains characteristic of the GPCR class.
source: Adhesion G-Protein Coupled Receptors, which have extracellular adhesion motifs and seven transmembrane domains characteristic of the GPCR class (lat-1, lat-2, cdh-6 in C. elegans [Mee et al., 2004; Willson et al., 2004; Hutter et al., 2000]), or components of the YAP/TAZ transcriptional program (Panciera et al., 2017) may integrate responses to forces transmitted via the cytoskeleton and could be considered as potential players in the required signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Mee et al., 2004; Willson et al., 2004; Hutter et al., 2000).

claim: Components of the YAP/TAZ transcriptional program may integrate responses to forces transmitted via the cytoskeleton.
source: Adhesion G-Protein Coupled Receptors, which have extracellular adhesion motifs and seven transmembrane domains characteristic of the GPCR class (lat-1, lat-2, cdh-6 in C. elegans [Mee et al., 2004; Willson et al., 2004; Hutter et al., 2000]), or components of the YAP/TAZ transcriptional program (Panciera et al., 2017) may integrate responses to forces transmitted via the cytoskeleton and could be considered as potential players in the required signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Panciera et al., 2017).

claim: Fluid injections, which require 2 min long sustained application of the filling stimulus to induce exophers, could provoke exopher production on a rapid timeframe, typically recorded only 10 min after the injection period.
source: Modeling will also need to incorporate the fact that fluid injections, which require 2 min long sustained application of the filling stimulus to induce exophers, could provoke exopher production on a rapid timeframe, typically recorded only 10 min after the injection period.

claim: The proteostressed touch neurons appear poised to eliminate contents upon mechanical stimulation.
source: Thus the proteostressed touch neurons appear poised to eliminate contents upon mechanical stimulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data in Figure 7 showing rapid exopher induction after injection.

claim: Distention of the female fly reproductive tract by egg passage through the tract (normal biology) or by artificial means (experimental fluid injection) can induce behavioral attraction of the mother to acetic acid, thought to signal a favorable food environment for offspring.
source: Distention of the female fly reproductive tract by egg passage through the tract (normal biology) or by artificial means (experimental fluid injection) can induce behavioral attraction of the mother to acetic acid, thought to signal a favorable food environment for offspring (Gou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Gou et al., 2014).

evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Gou et al., 2014).

claim: Uterine stretch in mammals has been reported to influence maternal behavior.
source: Uterine stretch in mammals has also been to reported influence maternal behavior (Kristal, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Kristal, 2009).

claim: Turek et al. report that exophers produced by C. elegans muscle cells follow a similar time course of highest production at adult day 2.
source: Turek et al. report that exophers produced by C. elegans muscle cells follow a similar time course of highest production at adult day 2, and demonstrated a dependence of the temporal muscle exophergenesis pattern on eggs, and commonly with highest exopher production in muscles in the vicinity of the uterus (Turek et al., 2021) (muscle exophers may be released to supply nutrients to developing progeny).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Turek et al., 2021).

claim: Turek et al. demonstrated a dependence of the temporal muscle exophergenesis pattern on eggs, and commonly with highest exopher production in muscles in the vicinity of the uterus.
source: Turek et al. report that exophers produced by C. elegans muscle cells follow a similar time course of highest production at adult day 2, and demonstrated a dependence of the temporal muscle exophergenesis pattern on eggs, and commonly with highest exopher production in muscles in the vicinity of the uterus (Turek et al., 2021) (muscle exophers may be released to supply nutrients to developing progeny).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Turek et al., 2021).

claim: Muscle exophers may be released to supply nutrients to developing progeny.
source: Turek et al. report that exophers produced by C. elegans muscle cells follow a similar time course of highest production at adult day 2, and demonstrated a dependence of the temporal muscle exophergenesis pattern on eggs, and commonly with highest exopher production in muscles in the vicinity of the uterus (Turek et al., 2021) (muscle exophers may be released to supply nutrients to developing progeny).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on citation (Turek et al., 2021).

claim: The onset of reproduction and the initial filling of the uterus triggers, or generates a 'license' for EV/exopher production across tissues.
